posts.title: AI This Week: ChatGPT Wallet Adds Checkout and 22 More Releases (Nov 9-15, 2026)
posts.description: ChatGPT Wallet lets agents pay after user approval, Claude Fable 5.2 takes the reasoning lead, and Google prices a million-token model for everyday coding work.
takeaways: OpenAI launched [ChatGPT Wallet](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/6825453-chatgpt-release-notes) on Nov 13, letting an agent complete a purchase after the buyer reviews the order and authorizes payment.
Anthropic released [Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2](https://www.anthropic.com/claude-fable-and-mythos-5-2) on Nov 9 at $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens.

Google released [Gemini 4 Hydrogen](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/models-and-research/gemini-models/introducing-gemini-4-hydrogen/) on Nov 12 with the same token rates across its full 1 million-token context window.

Microsoft made [Bring Your Own Model](https://devblogs.microsoft.com/visualstudio/bring-your-own-model-is-now-generally-available-in-visual-studio/) generally available in Visual Studio 18.12 on Nov 11, including support for local models.

Salesforce released [SOV-Transcribe-1](https://huggingface.co/salesforce-sovereign-intelligence/SOV-Transcribe-1) on Nov 12, an open-weight transcription model with 26.6 billion total parameters and 4.6 billion active parameters.
Three WhichAI.today categories changed leaders on Nov 12: [reasoning](/changes/2026-11-12-reasoning), [general use](/changes/2026-11-12-general), and [web research](/changes/2026-11-12-research).

sections.heading: ChatGPT Wallet adds checkout, with the buyer approving each order
paragraphs: OpenAI released [ChatGPT Wallet](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/6825453-chatgpt-release-notes) on Nov 13. A ChatGPT agent can now do more than find a product: it can complete checkout without seeing the buyer’s actual card details. The initial [Wallet rollout](https://openai.com/index/introducing-chatgpt-wallet/) is narrower than the product name suggests. It starts in dots, OpenAI’s personal agents, for US ChatGPT Pro subscribers aged 18 or older with an eligible US-issued card.

The buyer still makes the spending decision. Before an order goes through, the buyer reviews the merchant, the items, the total, and the selected card, then approves the purchase with a security check such as a fingerprint scan. The payment network supplies a substitute credential for checkout; the charge goes to the selected card, but neither the agent nor the merchant gets its actual number. ([openai.com](https://openai.com/index/introducing-chatgpt-wallet/))

That approval covers a particular order, not an ongoing shopping assignment. Under the [ChatGPT Wallet terms](https://openai.com/policies/chatgpt-wallet-terms/), a material change before submission requires fresh approval. The merchant remains the seller and sets the return policy. For someone delegating a purchase, the practical dividing line is straightforward: the agent can handle checkout, but it cannot treat approval of one price as permission to pay another.

OpenAI addressed the seller’s side on Nov 10 with [Businesses in ChatGPT](https://openai.com/business/businesses-in-chatgpt/). A business can claim its profile, and eligible US e-commerce and online service businesses can publish an agent that answers questions from the company’s product and policy information. The [business setup guide](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/20001635-setting-up-your-business-on-chatgpt) distinguishes claiming a profile from qualifying for an agent. For a retailer, keeping a return policy accurate and accepting an approved payment are two separate jobs.

sections.heading: Claude gains speed while Gemini and Qwen offer million-token context
paragraphs: Anthropic’s Nov 9 update to [Claude Fable and Claude Mythos](https://www.anthropic.com/claude-fable-and-mythos-5-2) combined lower prices with reported improvements in coding, reasoning, and vision. The company says the 5.2 models generate output up to 30% faster than their respective 5.1 predecessors. That measures how quickly an answer is written, not how quickly an entire assignment finishes: a coding job can also spend time waiting for a tool or running tests.

Google took a different approach with [Gemini 4 Hydrogen](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/models-and-research/gemini-models/introducing-gemini-4-hydrogen/) on Nov 12. Hydrogen is built to carry out steps in coding and other agent workflows. It costs $1.50 per million input tokens and $7.50 per million output tokens, with no price jump as a request approaches the 1 million-token limit. That makes the input bill easier to estimate for jobs that vary from a few files to a large collection.

The price difference is easiest to see on a sample workload. At the announced rates, 100,000 input tokens and 10,000 output tokens cost $0.225 on Hydrogen versus $1.20 on either Claude 5.2 model, counting token charges alone. That example holds the amount of text constant; it does not assume the models require the same number of attempts. For a repeated job, the more useful figure is the cost of an answer someone can actually use.

Alibaba Cloud’s [Qwen4-Max-Preview](https://www.alibabacloud.com/help/en/model-studio/qwen4-max-preview) also arrived with a 1 million-token window on Nov 11. It combines text generation, image and video understanding, reasoning, and tool calls. The distinction for teams planning a rollout is availability: Qwen4-Max was a preview during the week, while [Hydrogen was available](/releases/2026-11-12-google-gemini-4-hydrogen). Neither model’s context limit, by itself, says how reliably it will find a detail buried in a long file.

Meta aimed its Nov 9 [Muse Ember](https://dev.meta.ai/resources/blog/build-with-muse-ember) release at smaller tasks performed often. Available in Muse Code and through the Meta Model API, the compact model accepts text, images, audio, and video for work including document analysis and coding subtasks. For a team sorting incoming material, an informative trial would give Ember the same request as a typed note, a photographed page, and a spoken message. That tests the feature Meta emphasized rather than rewarding the longest answer.

sections.heading: Coding tools add parallel agents, local models, and access to app features
paragraphs: Google introduced [/swarm in Antigravity](https://antigravity.google/blog/gemini-4-carbon-in-google-antigravity/) in preview on Nov 10 alongside the rollout of Gemini 4 Carbon in the coding environment. The command coordinates specialized agents that can plan, write code, and verify work in parallel. The change is in how an assignment is divided: a developer can give the team a shared objective rather than manually passing one assistant’s plan to another for implementation.

Microsoft’s Nov 11 release of [Bring Your Own Model in Visual Studio 18.12](https://devblogs.microsoft.com/visualstudio/bring-your-own-model-is-now-generally-available-in-visual-studio/) answers a different question: which model gets to do the work? Developers can connect a custom endpoint or a local model without leaving the editor. The distinction matters for a team that already operates an approved model. It can evaluate the editor integration without also having to evaluate a new model provider.

For people building applications rather than modifying an existing codebase, Google added [Google Maps Platform to AI Studio](https://developers.googleblog.com/from-prompt-to-app-build-with-google-maps-in-ai-studio/) on Nov 9. Developers can prompt Gemini to build a store locator, route planner, or air-quality display using Maps services. The sandbox has quotas and does not require a credit card. That is a useful distinction for a prototype: a team can test whether the map answers its users’ question before making a production spending decision.

DeepSeek’s Nov 13 [App API release](https://api-docs.deepseek.com/news/news261113/) brought web search, URL reading, file input, speech recognition, and text-to-speech out of its chat app and into its developer offering. Consider a support application that needs to read an attached manual and a customer-supplied web page. Those are now capabilities its developer can call directly; the customer need not be sent to the DeepSeek chat interface to perform those steps.

sections.heading: Meeting assistants, live translation, and open-weight transcription
paragraphs: On Nov 11, xAI added [meetings and calls to Grok Bot](https://x.ai/changelog/bot). On Team, Enterprise, and Ultra plans, a bot can join from a Google Meet, Zoom, or Microsoft Teams link, answer questions in meeting chat, and send a summary afterward. For an organization whose customers choose the conferencing platform, support for all three is a more useful starting criterion than a comparison of sample summaries from just one.

Anthropic’s [Claude Meetings](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/12138966-release-notes) entered beta on Nov 12 for Team and Enterprise plans. It joins Google Meet as a visible participant and can create a document, whiteboard, or slide deck during the conversation. That gives the two meeting assistants distinct uses: Grok covers three call platforms, while Claude offers a way for participants on a Meet call to inspect a draft together instead of waiting for the minutes.

Two days earlier, Anthropic introduced [Sheets and Whiteboards templates](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/17153992-what-are-artifacts-and-how-do-i-use-them) for collaborative work inside Claude. The beta covers Pro, Max, Ultra, Team, and Enterprise plans, but the administrative defaults differ: the templates are on for Team and off for Enterprise until an owner enables them. A company preparing a workshop should check that setting before promising participants a shared board.

DeepL’s [Aure](https://www.deepl.com/en/press-release/aure-voice-ai-model), released Nov 11, tackles the conversation itself rather than its written record. The real-time voice translation model covers eight languages and is designed to preserve rhythm, intonation, and tone. For a multilingual presentation, a useful listening test would include a question, a correction, and an emphatic answer: the words matter in all three, but so does the way the speaker delivers them.

Salesforce’s Nov 12 [SOV-Transcribe-1 model card](https://huggingface.co/salesforce-sovereign-intelligence/SOV-Transcribe-1) describes a different speech job: turning recorded audio into text, not translating a live exchange. The Apache 2.0 open-weight model supports multilingual transcription, guidance on writing style, and context to favor relevant terms. Its 26.6 billion total parameters include 4.6 billion active parameters. For a team transcribing interviews with unusual names, the terminology feature is a reason to test it; for live captions, its non-streaming design is a reason to look elsewhere.

sections.heading: Enterprise releases change how companies buy, host, and assign AI work
paragraphs: On Nov 9, OpenAI made [ChatGPT Enterprise available in AWS Marketplace](https://openai.com/index/chatgpt-enterprise-aws-marketplace/). Organizations can purchase and manage seats through their existing Amazon Web Services billing relationship, and eligible spending can count toward AWS commitments. This changes the purchasing route, not the model employees use. The word to check in a budget review is “eligible,” rather than assuming the entire purchase will offset a commitment.

Anthropic’s Nov 12 [self-hosted Claude Managed Agents release](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/release-notes/overview) concerns where the service runs after a company adopts it. Organizations can host the whole Managed Agents service on their own infrastructure, including agents, sessions, and session history, rather than hosting only the sandboxes that execute work. It is an agent-service deployment option, not an announcement that Claude model weights can be downloaded.

Databricks introduced [Always-on Genie](https://www.databricks.com/company/newsroom/press-releases/databricks-launches-new-always-genie-autonomous-ai-complex) on Nov 11 as a second-generation agent for work across enterprise data and business systems. The proposed change is from asking a question on demand to assigning work to a persistent agent. A useful pilot would start with a recurring task that has a clear finish line, then check both the result and which steps still needed a person.

Google Cloud’s Nov 10 [Gemini for healthcare](https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/ai-machine-learning/gemini-for-healthcare) is more specific about the systems involved: clinical, financial, administrative, and insurance workflows, including electronic health records. Its purpose is to coordinate multi-step tasks without asking staff to switch applications at every handoff. For an operations team, the relevant demonstration is a handoff across the systems it actually uses, not a general medical question answered in a chat window.

sections.heading: Creative tools, robotics, and genomics get task-specific updates
paragraphs: Adobe made two distinct releases on Nov 10. Its [Creative Cloud update](https://news.adobe.com/news/2026/11/adobe-transforms-creative-cloud-tools) added Creative Agent, Relight, Color Mode, and co-editing tools. For an art director reviewing an existing composition, the useful distinction is between proposing a revision and controlling the result: lighting and color are concrete changes that collaborators can inspect rather than judging an entirely new image.

The separate [Firefly AI Creative Studio update](https://news.adobe.com/news/2026/11/adobe-firefly-expands) added Quick Actions, Firefly Graph, and tools for video, design, and image editing alongside Creative Agent. Creative Agent appears in both announcements, so its presence alone does not distinguish the products. A team choosing what to trial can start with the deliverable: a jointly edited composition points toward the Creative Cloud update, while a project moving between image, design, and video work gives Firefly a clearer test.

Google DeepMind released [Gemini Robotics 2.5](https://deepmind.google/models/gemini-robotics/) on Nov 10. It is a vision-language-action model: the intended output is a robot’s action, not a written description of what the robot sees. Google describes support for bodies ranging from paired arms to humanoids. For a robotics team, that breadth makes its own hardware and task the right test; support for a body shape is not a success rate for a particular movement.

On Nov 11, Google DeepMind released [AlphaGenome 2](https://deepmind.google/blog/alphagenome-2-deciphering-how-cells-read-dna-to-better-understand-disease/), trained on more than 100 million individual cell profiles across 68 tissues. The team reports that it identified nearly twice as many variants linked to gene expression in specific human cell types as the previous model. The unit of comparison matters: the reported gain concerns identifying those links, not doubling the accuracy of every prediction or establishing a diagnosis for a patient.

sections.heading: Fable, Carbon, and Qwen take three different ranking leads
paragraphs: Claude Fable 5.2 replaced Claude Opus 5.5 at the top of [Reasoning, Math & Science on Nov 12](/changes/2026-11-12-reasoning), scoring 74.3% on Humanity’s Last Exam. The [benchmark authors](https://www.lastexam.ai/) describe 2,500 closed-ended questions across more than 100 subjects. That is evidence about solving difficult academic problems with checkable answers, not a claim that Fable gets 74.3% of an employee’s daily assignments right.

Fable 5.2 also ended the week first in [Coding & Software](/coding), with 1,838 on LMArena Code against 1,764 for GPT-6 Astra. Coding was not one of the three recorded leadership changes. Nor did the new version displace its predecessor everywhere: [Legal & Long Documents](/legal) still listed Fable 5.1 at 88.5 on Vals LegalBench, tied at the top of that benchmark.

Google’s Gemini 4 Carbon replaced Gemini 4 Argon in [General & Everyday on Nov 12](/changes/2026-11-12-general) with an overall LMArena Text score of 1,526. Argon nevertheless retained the [Writing & Marketing lead](/writing) with 1,523 on the creative-writing board. A team choosing a drafting assistant has a reason to keep testing Argon even if Carbon is its first pick for a mixed set of everyday questions.

Alibaba’s Qwen3.8-Max took [Research & Web Search on Nov 12](/changes/2026-11-12-research), scoring 1,260 on LMArena Search against 1,258 for the previous leader, GPT-5.6 Sol. The two-point difference establishes the order in this week’s snapshot, not a large practical advantage. It was Qwen3.8-Max that earned the ranking, not the similarly named [Qwen4-Max-Preview released Nov 11](/releases/2026-11-11-alibaba-cloud-qwen4-max-preview).

faqs.question: Who could use ChatGPT Wallet at its Nov 13 launch?
faqs.answer: The initial rollout covered US ChatGPT Pro subscribers aged 18 or older using dots with an eligible US-issued card. The buyer had to review and approve each purchase; saving a card did not give the agent permission to spend freely.

faqs.question: How much did Gemini 4 Hydrogen and Claude 5.2 cost at launch?
faqs.answer: Gemini 4 Hydrogen launched at $1.50 per million input tokens and $7.50 per million output tokens across its 1 million-token context window. Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 launched at $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens.

faqs.question: Which AI meeting assistant supported Zoom, Teams, and Google Meet?
faqs.answer: As of Nov 11, Grok Bot could join all three platforms on xAI’s Team, Enterprise, and Ultra plans. Claude Meetings entered beta on Nov 12 for Google Meet on Team and Enterprise plans, with the ability to make documents, whiteboards, and slides during a call.

faqs.question: Which open-weight speech model was released during Nov 9-15?
faqs.answer: Salesforce released SOV-Transcribe-1 on Nov 12 under Apache 2.0. It is a multilingual, non-streaming transcription model with 26.6 billion total parameters and 4.6 billion active parameters, intended for recorded audio rather than live translation.

faqs.question: Which AI models moved into first place on Nov 12?
faqs.answer: Claude Fable 5.2 took the reasoning lead, Gemini 4 Carbon took the general-use lead, and Qwen3.8-Max took the web-research lead. Their respective scores were 74.3% on Humanity’s Last Exam, 1,526 on LMArena Text overall, and 1,260 on LMArena Search.

posts.title: AI This Week: Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash Takes the Video Lead (Nov 2-8, 2026)
posts.description: Google took the video and writing leads as OpenAI added GIFs, Cursor shipped live app hosting, and five open-weight releases landed in the week’s 29 AI updates.
takeaways: Google released [Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/technology/developers-tools/introducing-gemini-omni-1-2-flash/) on Nov 5 with 15-second video generation and 30% lower pricing; it took the [video lead](/changes/2026-11-06-video) on Nov 6.
OpenAI released [Images 2.6](https://openai.com/index/introducing-images-2-6/) on Nov 4 with animated GIF creation and a company-reported 50% increase in image generation speed.
Cognition released [SWE-2 Flash](https://cognition.com/blog/swe-2-flash) on Nov 4 at one-fifth the price and three times the speed of SWE-2, according to the company.

Cursor added [live app deployment](https://cursor.com/changelog/build-live-apps) on Nov 5, letting a cloud agent build a web app, configure its database and authentication, and share the hosted result.
Preferred Networks released [PLaMo 3 Translate](https://www.preferred.jp/en/blog/tech/plamo-3-translate-weight-release) on Nov 5 in four open-weight sizes for offline translation across 53 languages.
Google’s Gemini 4 Argon displaced Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5.5 in [Writing & Marketing](/changes/2026-11-08-writing) on Nov 8, the second of the week’s two ranking changes.

sections.heading: Google’s 15-second video model took first place a day after release
paragraphs: Google’s [Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/technology/developers-tools/introducing-gemini-omni-1-2-flash/) gave video makers three concrete reasons to reconsider their tools on Nov 5: native 15-second clips with audio, the ability to revise them through conversation, and 30% lower pricing. On Nov 6 it replaced Gemini Omni 1.1 Flash at the top of the [Video ranking](/changes/2026-11-06-video). This was an upgrade to the incumbent, not a change of vendor.

For someone preparing a short product spot, the editing change matters at least as much as the extra room for a scene. The task is rarely finished with the first generation: a reviewer might like the shot but want the action to start sooner. Conversational editing makes that a revision request, while native audio lets the reviewer judge picture and sound together. Google also reports stronger consistency; keeping the approved parts intact through a revision is a useful way to test that claim.

The ranking supplies a separate piece of evidence. The Nov 6 change was recorded at 1541 on LMArena Text-to-Video; the [Video standings](/video) list the model at 1540. Both figures place it first, but the benchmark is for text-to-video output. It does not establish which tool is cheapest for a finished campaign or which one follows a particular editor’s revision notes most faithfully.

OpenAI’s Nov 4 [Images 2.6 release](https://openai.com/index/introducing-images-2-6/) serves a different brief. It added animated GIF creation across a rollout spanning ChatGPT, Codex, and the API, and OpenAI says it generates images 50% faster than before. The API versions are GPT-Image-2.6 Flare and Sunburst. For a looping illustration rather than a clip with sound, GIF output is the more relevant addition, even though it did not produce a change atop the [Images ranking](/images).

sections.heading: Coding agents got cheaper runs, live app hosting, and voice calls
paragraphs: Cognition made [SWE-2 Flash](https://cognition.com/blog/swe-2-flash) available in Devin Desktop and CLI on Nov 4. Its comparison is unusually easy to interpret: the company quotes one-fifth the price and three times the speed of its larger SWE-2 model. That is a comparison with one sibling, not with every coding assistant, and it is a reason to try Flash on repeated edits rather than assume the two models solve equally difficult problems.

Cursor changed what a coding agent can hand back. With [Build Live Apps](https://cursor.com/changelog/build-live-apps), released Nov 5, its cloud agents can build an app, set up a Postgres database, configure authentication, and deploy the result behind a shareable link. A colleague reviewing an internal prototype can try the running app instead of reading a code change or asking the author to demonstrate it. For that handoff, whether the right people can sign in is as important as whether the page renders.

On Nov 6, Cursor added [two-way voice chat with agents](https://cursor.com/changelog/voice-chat) in its Agents Window, IDE, web interface, and iOS app. It is a live conversation rather than just speech-to-text input: a developer can ask what the agent is doing and hear its response. GitHub’s Nov 4 [Copilot integration with Xcode’s built-in coding assistant](https://github.blog/changelog/2026-11-04-github-copilot-is-now-available-in-xcodes-coding-assistant/) took another route to reducing interruptions. That integration was a public preview starting with Xcode 27.3 beta, not a feature of every Xcode installation.

Security teams had a separate model release on Nov 5. OpenAI introduced [GPT-6 Cyber](https://openai.com/index/introducing-gpt-6-cyber/) for finding and fixing software vulnerabilities, reporting better adherence to the scope set by an authorized researcher. Its Nov 4 [Daybreak Red announcement](https://openai.com/index/daybreak-red-aws-govcloud/) concerned a different model and a specific deployment: approved customers could access GPT-5.6 Cyber through Amazon Bedrock in AWS GovCloud (US-East). The distinction matters for procurement: the GovCloud announcement was not a GPT-6 Cyber availability notice.

sections.heading: Five open-weight releases ranged from offline translation to research
paragraphs: Preferred Networks made the most direct pitch to people with a specific job to do. Its Nov 5 [PLaMo 3 Translate release](https://www.preferred.jp/en/blog/tech/plamo-3-translate-weight-release) covers 53 languages and comes in four sizes, from 0.8 billion to 31 billion parameters. The models can translate offline. For a team that needs to keep documents on its own equipment, the useful comparison is how each size handles the team’s language pairs and terminology on the hardware it actually has.

At the other end of the size range, Deep Principle released [Hydrogen-1.0](https://huggingface.co/deep-principle/Hydrogen-1.0) on Nov 2. Based on GLM-5.3, the scientific research model has approximately 753 billion parameters and a 1-million-token context window. Ricursive Intelligence’s Nov 4 [Ripple-65B Preview](https://huggingface.co/ricursiveAI/Ripple-65B-Preview) also takes long inputs, but targets coding and reasoning with a 65-billion-parameter dense model. Its weights were available despite “Preview” in the name, and its specified limit is exactly 1,048,576 tokens.

Ripple’s model card reports training on 12 trillion tokens and a score of 80.52 on TerminalBench 2.1. Those numbers answer different questions from the context limit: one describes the amount of training material, one a coding evaluation, and one how much material fits into a request. A team choosing between Ripple and Hydrogen for a long technical project has better evidence in their respective task descriptions than in the fact that both advertise roughly a million tokens.

Baidu’s Nov 5 [ERNIE 5.5 Flash Base](https://huggingface.co/baidu/ERNIE-5.5-Flash-Base) is a foundation model with 280 billion parameters, of which 14 billion are active per token. Baidu specifies up to 128,000 tokens of context during pretraining and support for 1 million during fine-tuning and inference. Sarvam AI’s Nov 3 [Sarvam Prism](https://www.sarvam.ai/blogs/sarvam-prism), the fifth open-weight entry in the week’s [release log](/releases), has a narrower purpose: making fast decisions. Sarvam built it on Sarvam 105B and released the weights so organizations can train it on their own data.

sections.heading: Decision models targeted milliseconds while larger models added more input types
paragraphs: Three announcements focused on choosing an answer quickly rather than composing a long one. Sarvam reported a 44-millisecond response for Prism on a B200 GPU on Nov 3. On Nov 4, Celeris released [Celeris-1.1 Decision](https://celeris.ai/), a diffusion-based model that makes categorical choices in about 40 milliseconds; it reported 80.2% on jev-bench and 76.2% on typed-decisions. The two latency figures are vendor measurements, not a common test that establishes a four-millisecond advantage.

Salesforce previewed [Koa Decisions](https://www.salesforce.com/news/stories/koa-decisions-salesforce-decision-models/?bc=OTH) on Nov 6. Built on Google’s Gemma architecture, it makes single-step routing choices from text, images, or audio in milliseconds. Consider a support queue: deciding which team should receive an incoming item is a different assignment from investigating it and writing a reply. The first task is the one these decision-model announcements address.

Tencent’s Nov 4 [Hy4 release](https://www.tencent.com/tencent-launches-hy4-joining-the-ranks-of-the-worlds-leading-open-source-ai-models/) paired visual understanding with reasoning and computer-use capabilities. Ant Group’s [Ling-3.2-flash](https://developer.ant-ling.com/en/docs/getting-started/changelog/), released Nov 5, accepts text, images, and video within a 1-million-token context window. It has 560 billion total parameters and uses 25 billion per token. For a job involving recorded footage, Ling’s explicit video support is more informative than the broad label “multimodal.”

Thinking Machines Lab also released [Inkling 2 Small](https://thinkingmachines.ai/news/inkling-2-small/) on Nov 5, with text and image input, variable effort, and access through Tinker Playground. “Small” is part of its name: the model has 594 billion total parameters and 17 billion active. Flower Labs’ Nov 3 [Endeavor 1.1 preview](https://flower.ai/blog/2026-11-03-introducing-endeavor-1.1) added native image input alongside dedicated EU GPU inference and reported improvements in reasoning and coding. For teams with a regional processing requirement, the location of inference may settle a shortlist before parameter counts enter the discussion.

sections.heading: Workplace agents gained persistent projects, scoped access, and cited search
paragraphs: Perplexity’s Nov 4 [Teammates preview](https://www.perplexity.ai/hub/blog/teammates-are-agents-for-complex-ongoing-work) is aimed at work that continues after the initial conversation. Its agents can monitor connected workplace tools, coordinate a project as priorities change, and present results for review. Mistral AI’s Nov 5 [Studio enterprise release](https://mistral.ai/news/build-with-studio/) puts the emphasis on running the process: managed agents, multi-step workflows, monitoring dashboards, organization-scoped memory, and limits on system access. A project owner looking for updates and an administrator deciding what the agent may see have different reasons to care about these releases.

Anthropic’s Nov 2 [message threads beta](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/message-threads) tackles a less visible cost of an extended exchange. The Messages API keeps conversation history on the server, so an application sends only new messages on later requests. Anthropic says the smaller requests can reduce the wait for the first token in long agent loops. OpenAI changed model selection rather than conversation storage on Nov 3, adding [GPT-6.1 Terra to dots](https://openai.com/index/introducing-dots/) so a dot can draw on different models for different parts of its work.

Adobe brought [CX Enterprise Coworker](https://news.adobe.com/news/2026/11/adobe-integrates-agentic-cx-enterprise-coworker-into-ai-platforms) into other AI products on Nov 4, including ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini for business. The change gives customer-experience teams another place to start an Adobe workflow rather than a new general-purpose model to evaluate. Amazon’s Nov 5 [Web Answer release for Bedrock AgentCore](https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2026/11/web-answer-amazon-bedrock/) is a tool for the agent itself: one call returns a synthesized answer with citations to current web sources.

For document readers, Adobe’s Nov 3 [web search in Acrobat AI Assistant](https://blog.adobe.com/en/publish/2026/11/03/web-search-now-available-in-acrobat) offers a related choice without requiring anyone to build an agent. A reader can ask about a document, bring in web sources when wanted, and inspect citations. That distinction is useful when reviewing a dated report: what the report originally said and what has happened since are two separate questions, even when the answers appear in the same conversation.

sections.heading: Classroom coaching and read-only finance gave assistants narrower jobs
paragraphs: Google made [Guided Learning globally available in Google Classroom](https://blog.google/products-and-platforms/products/education/ai-learning-era-updates-2026/) on Nov 3. A teacher assigns the activity, and the assistant uses class material to coach the student step by step instead of simply providing the answer. For a teacher comparing it with an ordinary chat session, the important detail is who sets the task and supplies the material: the activity starts with the lesson, not a blank prompt.

Anthropic previewed [Personal Finance in Claude](https://claude.com/resources/articles/introducing-personal-finance-in-claude) on Nov 5. People choose which accounts to connect and can ask about spending, balances, and transactions in everyday language. Access is read-only: explaining where money went is within the feature’s scope; moving it is not. That boundary distinguishes this preview from the week’s agents that can take actions such as deploying an app.

Meta began rolling out [specialized models for Muse and Meta AI](https://research.meta.ai/blog/specialized-models-for-muse-and-metaai) on Nov 6. The company trained versions of existing models using Muse Wonder to deliver Active Memory and Active Focus. Unlike Anthropic’s message threads, which change what developers send to an API, this was an update to the assistants people use. The two announcements should not be read as equivalent claims about how either service stores conversations.

sections.heading: Gemini 4 Argon overtook Claude Opus 5.5 in writing
paragraphs: The week’s second ranking change came on Nov 8, when [Gemini 4 Argon replaced Claude Opus 5.5](/changes/2026-11-08-writing) in Writing & Marketing. The change record cites 1525 on LMArena Creative Writing. The [writing standings](/writing) list Argon at 1523 and Opus at 1517. The former number documents the lead change; the latter pair is the comparison to use when quoting the standings.

For a marketing team, the result makes Argon a candidate for drafting and tone work, not an automatic choice for every step in producing a campaign. A useful comparison would give Argon and Opus the same brief, then ask both to shorten the copy without losing the required claims or changing the brand voice. That tests the revision work a team actually buys; the creative-writing score supplies a starting point rather than a verdict on its copy.

Across the [29 releases](/releases), only [two category leads changed](/changes): Video and Writing & Marketing. Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5.2 remained first in [Coding & Software](/coding) at 1838 on LMArena Code, while OpenAI’s GPT-Image-2.5 Sunburst remained first in [Images](/images) at 1428 on LMArena Text-to-Image. The practical choice this week was sometimes a new feature rather than a new leader: a team needing GIF output had a reason to try Images 2.6 without claiming that it had already won the image benchmark.

faqs.question: Which AI model ranked first for video during Nov 2-8, 2026?
faqs.answer: Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash replaced Gemini Omni 1.1 Flash on Nov 6, one day after release. The change was recorded at 1541 on LMArena Text-to-Video; the standings list it at 1540.

faqs.question: Which open-weight AI models were released that week?
faqs.answer: Five releases were classified as open weights: Hydrogen-1.0, Sarvam Prism, Ripple-65B Preview, PLaMo 3 Translate, and ERNIE 5.5 Flash Base. Their intended uses range from scientific research and coding to quick decisions and offline translation.

faqs.question: What changed for developers using Cursor or Devin?
faqs.answer: Cursor added hosted web app deployment on Nov 5 and two-way voice calls with agents on Nov 6. Cognition released SWE-2 Flash in Devin Desktop and CLI on Nov 4, reporting three times the speed of SWE-2 at one-fifth the price.

faqs.question: Did GPT-6 Cyber launch in AWS GovCloud that week?
faqs.answer: The Nov 4 GovCloud announcement specified GPT-5.6 Cyber for approved customers in AWS GovCloud (US-East) through Amazon Bedrock. OpenAI’s Nov 5 GPT-6 Cyber model launch was a separate announcement.

faqs.question: Which AI model led the writing rankings on Nov 8, 2026?
faqs.answer: Gemini 4 Argon took first place in Writing & Marketing from Claude Opus 5.5 on Nov 8. The change record gives Argon a creative-writing score of 1525, while the standings list Argon at 1523 and Opus at 1517.

posts.title: AI This Week: GPT-6.1 Terra Halves Standard API Prices (Oct 26–Nov 1, 2026)
posts.description: GPT-6.1 Terra launched at half its predecessor’s standard API prices, Google previewed Gemini 4 Carbon, and Mistral released trillion-parameter model weights.
takeaways: OpenAI released [GPT-6.1 Terra](https://openai.com/index/introducing-gpt-6-1-terra/) on Oct 26 at standard API prices 50% below both GPT-5.6 Terra and GPT-6.1 Sol.

Google announced [Gemini 4 Carbon](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/models-and-research/gemini-models/introducing-gemini-4-carbon/) on Oct 28, with initial access limited to selected cyber defenders rather than a general rollout.

GitHub made [Copilot Fusion](https://github.blog/changelog/2026-10-28-route-and-orchestrate-models-with-github-copilot-fusion/) generally available on Oct 28, letting developers delegate model selection and coordination for coding tasks.

Mistral AI released the weights of its improved [Mistral Large 4](https://mistral.ai/news/mistral-large-4-oss/) on Oct 29, following an earlier public preview of the 1-trillion-parameter multimodal model.
NVIDIA released [Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe](https://huggingface.co/blog/nvidia/nemotron-transcribe-granary) on Oct 28 with transcription in 40 languages, speaker attribution and word-level timestamps.
Meituan released [LongCat-2.5](https://longcat.ai/blog/longcat-2.5) on Nov 1 with 1.6 trillion total parameters and about 48 billion active per token.
WhichAI.today tracked [31 releases](/releases) from Oct 26 through Nov 1 but recorded [no ranking changes](/changes) across its nine job categories.

sections.heading: GPT-6.1 Terra cuts the price of working from a screen
paragraphs: OpenAI released [GPT-6.1 Terra](https://openai.com/index/introducing-gpt-6-1-terra/) on Oct 26 at half the standard API prices of GPT-5.6 Terra and GPT-6.1 Sol. The combination that matters for office work is visual reasoning and computer use: reading an invoice is one step; finding the corresponding fields in accounting software and entering the figures is another. Terra is designed to do both.

OpenAI also published a comparison that goes beyond the price of a token. On Agents’ Last Exam, a test that includes professional tasks such as working from architectural drawings, Terra scored 15 percentage points above GPT-5.6 Terra at medium reasoning effort, at about one-third the cost. That is a result on OpenAI’s reported test, not a forecast that every accounting or design team will cut its bill by two-thirds. ([openai.com](https://openai.com/index/introducing-gpt-6-1-terra/))

For a team deciding whether to switch, the useful comparison is cost per correctly completed job. Give both models the same set of invoices, including some with missing fields, and count how many records a reviewer can accept without correction. That separates the price reduction, which applies to standard API rates, from the savings a team might actually see after retries and review. ChatGPT Work and Codex users have a different measure: OpenAI says the same usage allowance covers more tasks with Terra. ([openai.com](https://openai.com/index/introducing-gpt-6-1-terra/))

Google made a related but distinct change on Oct 30: its [Computer Use tool](https://aistudio.google.com/docs/changelog?auto_signin=false) reached general availability in both the Gemini Interactions and GenerateContent APIs. OpenAI’s announcement gives teams a new model and a specific price comparison. Google’s gives developers already building with those two APIs a generally available tool for interacting with computer interfaces.

sections.heading: Gemini 4 Carbon enters a limited preview as coding tools offer more model choice
paragraphs: Google introduced [Gemini 4 Carbon](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/models-and-research/gemini-models/introducing-gemini-4-carbon/) on Oct 28, emphasizing cybersecurity, coding and work that takes many steps to complete. Google said a subset of cyber defenders would receive access first, with other trusted partners to follow. Carbon’s 1,526 score on the [general-purpose ranking](/general) made it a model to watch, but not one that every team could adopt that week.

Developers who wanted a change they could use immediately got one on the same day. [GitHub Copilot Fusion](https://github.blog/changelog/2026-10-28-route-and-orchestrate-models-with-github-copilot-fusion/) became generally available on Oct 28. Rather than asking a developer to pick a model before tackling a coding task, Fusion can choose and coordinate multiple models. The decision shifts from choosing one model for the whole job to deciding whether to delegate that choice.

Microsoft’s [managed agent execution system for Foundry Agent Service](https://devblogs.microsoft.com/foundry/microsoft-copilot-harness-in-foundry/) entered public preview on Oct 28. It is aimed at developers building agents that use tools and work through long-running tasks across models. The distinction from Fusion is who is doing the building: a developer can select Fusion inside a coding product, while a team using Foundry is building an agent for its own application.

Particle AI offered a third approach on Oct 28. Its [Particle-1 coding model](https://particle.ai/blog/introducing-particle-1) builds on DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, and the company reported that it used about 45% fewer tokens on average across the tasks it tested. That figure describes token consumption, not a 45% improvement in accuracy or a guaranteed reduction in development time. A useful comparison would count both the tokens spent on a change and whether the resulting code passes review.

On Nov 1, Meituan released [LongCat-2.5](https://longcat.ai/blog/longcat-2.5), focused on visual coding and tasks that require an agent to keep working across multiple steps. Its 1.6 trillion total parameters describe the full model; about 48 billion are active for each token. For someone evaluating its visual coding, a more revealing test than model size would be to give it a screen design, ask for an implementation and compare the rendered result with the original.

sections.heading: Open weights range from a trillion-parameter flagship to models for edge devices
paragraphs: Mistral AI released the weights of [Mistral Large 4, also called Le Chonk](https://mistral.ai/news/mistral-large-4-oss/), on Oct 29. The 1-trillion-parameter model had already been in public preview; the week’s news was that teams could obtain the improved weights. Mistral reported a 13-percentage-point gain over its preview on Terminal-Bench 4.0, to 41%, while using 30% fewer output tokens on that test. The comparison is with its own preview, not with the leader on WhichAI.today’s coding board.

At the other end of the size range, Liquid AI released [LFM3](https://www.liquid.ai/blog/lfm3) on Oct 27. Its six open-weight models are all in the 2-billion-parameter class and share a common base, but they do different jobs: text, vision, audio, combined inputs and two forms of decision-making. For a team building a device that needs to make a limited choice rather than sustain a conversation, those last two models deserve a separate evaluation from the text model.

Long inputs were another reason to look beyond the flagship. InclusionAI released [Ling-3.1-flash-1019](https://huggingface.co/inclusionAI/Ling-3.1-flash-1019) on Oct 27 with a 1-million-token context window, 560 billion total parameters and 25 billion active per token. On Oct 30, NVIDIA published an [NVFP4 version of DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017](https://huggingface.co/nvidia/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017-NVFP4) with multimodal input and the same maximum context length. NVIDIA’s release is a lower-precision version of an existing model, not a new generation of DeepSeek.

Two releases shared a 35-billion-parameter headline without offering the same thing. On Oct 28, Apex Intelligence released its first model, [Apex-35B-V1.0](https://www.apexin.com/apex-35b/), a general-purpose model developed through additional training of an existing base. DiffuSpace released [Clover-35B-A3B-Preview](https://huggingface.co/Diffuspace/Clover-35B-A3B-Preview) on Oct 30 with a 128,000-token context window. Clover uses block diffusion to generate text and activates about 3 billion parameters per token; its weights were available despite the word “Preview” in its name.

Some teams do not need generated text at all. FrontiersMind’s Oct 29 [Lumma-Fev-v2 release](https://huggingface.co/blog/FrontiersMind/lumma-fev-27b-v2) offered 4-billion- and 27-billion-parameter models that score each supplied option in one pass, with room for 8,192 tokens of context. Nace AI’s [Drex Max v1](https://huggingface.co/nace-ai/drex-max-v1), released Nov 1, takes text, JSON or images and returns option probabilities from a 27-billion-parameter model. For a queue that routes documents to named departments, a score for each department is a more direct output than a paragraph someone must interpret.

sections.heading: Speech releases split into translation, transcription and conversation
paragraphs: For a bilingual meeting, the first decision is whether participants need to hear a translation as someone speaks or read a transcript afterward. Tencent released [Hy-SimulMT-30B-A3B](https://huggingface.co/tencent/Hy-SimulMT-30B-A3B) on Oct 26 for the first job: simultaneous speech-to-speech translation from Chinese to English and from English to Chinese. The 30-billion-parameter model has open weights under Apache 2.0 and produces translation-only output rather than acting as a general conversational assistant.

Microsoft’s Oct 26 [Azure AI Speech LLM 09-2026 update](https://devblogs.microsoft.com/foundry/announcing-azure-ai-speech-llm-09-2026/) addressed transcription. It added 25 languages and, according to Microsoft, processes speech up to twice as fast as version 2607 while improving accuracy. The 25 is the number of languages added, not the service’s total; the speed figure is an upper bound, not a promise that every recording will finish in half the time.

On Oct 28, NVIDIA released [Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe](https://huggingface.co/blog/nvidia/nemotron-transcribe-granary), an open-weight model that transcribes 40 languages. An instruction can request verbatim speech or a written-form transcript, identify speakers and attach timestamps to words. Those options suit different uses of the same recording: an editor checking a quotation needs the speaker’s actual words and their location, while a colleague reading meeting notes may prefer written form.

Rime’s [Prism](https://www.rime.ai/resources/prism-first-speech-to-speech-for-enterprise), released Oct 28, is for spoken exchanges rather than transcripts. Rime reported a response time of about 500 milliseconds and said an application can inspect a text layer before the model speaks. On Oct 29, ServiceNow previewed [Apriel Voice 27B](https://huggingface.co/ServiceNow-AI/Apriel-Voice-27B-preview), which accepts spoken requests but produces text and tool calls. A spoken input does not necessarily mean a spoken reply.

IBM released [Granite Switch 4.1.1](https://huggingface.co/blog/ibm-granite/granite-switch-4-1-1) on Oct 29. This was a patch, with updated speech-to-text support across 10 languages and a revised decision adapter. For an existing Granite deployment, the useful check is narrow: run recordings from the languages actually used at work, then check the resulting decisions separately rather than treating the patch as an entirely new voice assistant.

sections.heading: Creative tools add live scene direction, 3D objects and edits across a whole deck
paragraphs: Google previewed [Genie 4](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/models-and-research/google-deepmind/introducing-genie-4/) on Oct 27. The research model generates an interactive environment with native audio and lets a person direct events in natural language while the simulation runs. The important distinction from a video generator is timing: instead of specifying the entire scene before rendering, the operator can decide what should happen next after seeing the scene unfold.

For teams that need a file rather than a live scene, Speridlabs released [Idol](https://huggingface.co/speridlabs/idol) on Oct 28. From one picture of an object, it generates a 3D representation containing up to 1,048,576 elements called Gaussians and saves the result as a standard `.ply` file. Speridlabs reports 7.2 GB of video memory for the model. A generated view of the back of an object should be treated as an estimate, not as evidence of what a single front-facing photo could not show.

Apple announced [Creator Studio AI features](https://www.apple.com/newsroom/2026/10/apple-creator-studio-adds-powerful-new-ai-features-and-even-more-creative-tools/) on Oct 27, including assistants for Logic Pro, Keynote, Pages and Numbers, plus Generate Fill in Pixelmator Pro. Google’s Oct 30 [Gemini update for Slides](https://www.google.com/sorry/index?continue=https://workspaceupdates.googleblog.com/2026/10/edit-entire-presentations-with-gemini-in-Google-Slides.html&q=EgQEmkwSGIiEr9cGIi1VYeRSIE8ZapdBdC6aQNKW72PTZRp9We9Aq87ftkvyhbrDLnx0cdBiAX_GCdEyAnJSWgFDYLve75OO9IrYaQ) was already available: one prompt in the side panel can change several slides or the entire deck. A presenter can ask for a visual style to match another presentation instead of describing the change slide by slide.

Baidu tackled the input side of document work on Oct 27 with [Unlimited OCR 2](https://huggingface.co/baidu/Unlimited-OCR-2). Its open-weight parser uses a moving attention window with sparse references to process long documents without a fixed parsing horizon. That is a claim about how far the parser can continue, not a guarantee that every table or caption is correct. A practical test is to inspect a table that crosses a page boundary, not just the first clean page.

sections.heading: Workplace AI gets more specific about the job and the user
paragraphs: Anthropic released its [Claude for Nonprofits plugin](https://claude.com/resources/articles/expanding-claude-for-nonprofits) on Oct 26 for verified nonprofit organizations. Its skills cover fundraising, grant research, marketing and hiring. For a small team comparing it with a general chat assistant, a useful trial would be to take one real funding opportunity and see whether the plugin helps staff produce a usable research brief, not just a plausible fundraising email.

On Oct 28, Anthropic added [ready-to-use artifacts for legal work](https://claude.com/resources/articles/introducing-artifacts-for-legal-work) to Claude for Legal. These interactive tools cover work such as contract review and regulatory tracking; teams can adapt them with their own data and connectors, then share them. That makes the reusable review tool, rather than one lawyer’s conversation, the unit of work. It is also a different claim from scoring well on a [legal reading benchmark](/legal).

OpenAI changed how some users reach an agent on Oct 28, when [texting a Dot agent](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/6825453-chatgpt-release-notes) began rolling out in beta to U.S. ChatGPT Pro users through iMessage or RCS. On Oct 29, its [GPT-6 Luna update](https://deploymentsafety.openai.com/gpt-6-luna-october-28-2026-addendum) targeted the answers themselves: shorter responses and less overly agreeable language. Luna had launched in ChatGPT on Oct 7; the Oct 29 entry was a behavior update, not its debut.

On Oct 30, OpenAI previewed [GPT-6 Rosalind Research](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/9624314-model-release-notes) for multistep life sciences research. It combines GPT-6 reasoning with scientific tools and safeguards designed for biological work. Its preview status matters for anyone comparing the week’s workplace products: unlike the nonprofit plugin and legal artifacts, Rosalind was not listed as generally available.

sections.heading: All nine job rankings hold despite 31 releases
paragraphs: WhichAI.today recorded [no ranking changes](/changes) from Oct 26 through Nov 1. Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5.2 led [coding and software](/coding) at 1,838 on LMArena Code, ahead of GPT-6 Astra at 1,764. It also led [reasoning, math and science](/reasoning) at 74.3 on Humanity’s Last Exam. These scores measure different tasks on different scales; the useful comparison is between models within one category.

For [legal and long documents](/legal), Claude Fable 5.1 was listed first at 88.5 on Vals LegalBench, tied at the top of that benchmark. Google’s Gemini 4 Argon led [writing and marketing](/writing) at 1,523, six points ahead of Claude Opus 5.5. Neither result measures the convenience of a legal artifact or a deck-wide edit. Those product features can change which tool fits a job even when the underlying leaderboard stays put.

Gemini 4 Carbon was listed first for [general and everyday work](/general) at 1,526, while Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite led [speed and high volume](/speed) with an output-speed score of 412. The [image ranking](/images) still favored GPT-Image-2.5 Sunburst at 1,428, and Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash led [video](/video) at 1,540. For [research and web search](/research), Alibaba’s Qwen3.8-Max scored 1,260 against GPT-5.6 Sol’s 1,258. The week changed several practical choices, from API prices to how slides can be edited, without producing a recorded change of leader.

faqs.question: How much cheaper was GPT-6.1 Terra than GPT-5.6 Terra?
faqs.answer: On Oct 26, OpenAI set GPT-6.1 Terra’s standard API prices 50% below those of both GPT-5.6 Terra and GPT-6.1 Sol. That comparison covers API rates, not the price of a ChatGPT subscription or the total cost of completing any particular job.

faqs.question: Was Gemini 4 Carbon available to everyone when Google announced it?
faqs.answer: No. Google announced Gemini 4 Carbon on Oct 28 with initial access for selected cyber defenders and a planned expansion to trusted partners. Google’s Oct 30 general-availability announcement concerned the separate Computer Use tool in two Gemini APIs.

faqs.question: Which open-weight AI models came out from Oct 26 to Nov 1, 2026?
faqs.answer: Highlights included Liquid AI’s six-model LFM3 family on Oct 27, NVIDIA’s Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe on Oct 28 and the improved Mistral Large 4 weights on Oct 29. Other releases served narrower jobs, including Tencent’s Chinese-English simultaneous translator, Baidu’s long-document parser and Nace AI’s Drex Max v1 decision model.

faqs.question: Which speech model could translate a live Chinese-English conversation?
faqs.answer: Tencent released Hy-SimulMT-30B-A3B on Oct 26 for simultaneous speech-to-speech translation in both directions between Chinese and English. For a written record with speaker labels and timestamps instead, NVIDIA’s Oct 28 Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe release supported transcription in 40 languages.

faqs.question: Did any AI model rankings change during the week?
faqs.answer: WhichAI.today recorded 31 releases and zero ranking changes across nine job categories from Oct 26 through Nov 1. Claude Fable 5.2 remained the coding leader, Gemini 4 Argon led writing, and Gemini 4 Carbon was listed first for general use.
